;redcode-94
;name G2-Clear
;author Unknown
;source https://corewar.co.uk/clear.htm
;strategy Simple clear loop with decrementing pointer
;assert CORESIZE == 8000 && MAXCYCLES == 80000

dec     equ     2700                ; Decrement value for bomb counter
gate    equ     clear-4             ; Gate location relative to clear

        org     clear-1             ; Start execution before clear

; Main data and bomb structures
bptr    dat     bomb,       9       ; Pointer to bomb with offset 9
bomb    spl     #dec,       11      ; Split with decrement value, creates processes
clear   mov     *bptr,      >gate   ; Move bomb contents through gate pointer
        mov     *bptr,      >gate   ; Second move for double clearing
        djn.f   clear,      }bomb   ; Decrement and jump if not zero (loop control)

        end

part.text:
I'm going to try a well-known strong warrior first, either a paper built around a scanner or a stone/imp design. I also want to test several classic designs, and I'm starting with a test script to compare them. Snake is mainly imp-spiral plus vampire, and imps tend to produce ties, so I need about 33% wins against it to make progress.

I'm planning to try a known strong warrior and a few classic designs, starting with a test harness to compare them.

input.command:
cd /app; cat > test.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
w=${1:-my_warrior.red}
for o in stone vampire paper snake g2-clear; do
  echo -n "$o: "; pmars -b -r 100 -f $w warriors/$o.red | tail -1
done
EOF
chmod +x test.sh; pmars -b -r 10 -f warriors/stone.red warriors/paper.red

I'm weighing whether paper's bombs can actually stop the g2-clear, since it only takes about 5 instructions to hit. Paper still loses eventually unless something kills g2, and imps tie the snake, so I need a way to deal with imps, perhaps by combining paper with a core clear or a better scanner.

Next I'm thinking about paper with anti-imp bombs, using a silk built around a bomb like `dat <2667, <5334`. I'll try a few bomb variants and step constants, and also look at a paper-plus-clear structure for dealing with the imps.

part.text:
Paper's weak spot is g2-clear, so I'm looking for something that can beat it, maybe a scanner or bomber that hits it early. g2-clear is tiny and clears forward from itself, with its gate at clear-4, which sits outside the program as a zero-filled cell whose B field gets incremented.

I'm still sorting out how g2-clear's bptr and bomb interact, since its writes seem to land on its own code. Its overall effect is unclear to me, but the result is that it beats paper. A quick scanner in front of paper, or a fast stone-style bomber, might work against its small footprint, though my stoneimp lost to it.

I'm weighing a quickscan combined with paper, since g2's five-instruction footprint is hard to hit by chance. I'm also wondering whether a paper variant that bombs in two places could catch g2's processes, since any hit on its three loop lines would eventually take them all out.

I'm tracing how g2-clear's bomb starts: the spl with an immediate A-field seems to split back onto itself, so its processes multiply at the bomb and feed into the clear loop. The bomb's A field gets bumped on each pass through the djn loop, which is where I'm getting stuck.

Now I'm weighing whether a known scanner design like Iron Gate could work here, since a well-tuned scan-and-bomb approach might find g2-clear's small footprint more reliably than a fixed bomber.

I'm thinking about writing a scanner that can be tuned against stone-style bombers, and I recall the Iron Gate design as a starting point. The next step I'm considering is a scan-and-clear approach that starts a spl/dat clear on any target it finds, since my earlier scanner lost to stone about 59% of the time.

I'm comparing a scanner against stone bombers, but the bombs in that setup are dat cells with nonzero B fields, so a scanner would mistake them for targets and waste cycles clearing them. I'm also thinking that paper's real gap is that it doesn't hit g2, which is the problem I need to solve.

I'm considering a more aggressive paper that bombs at more than one spot, such as a variant using `mov.i #x, <y` to hit anti-imp positions. part.text:
I've written `/app/my_warrior.red`, and it beats every target when run with the exact test command (`pmars -b -r 100 -f my_warrior.red warriors/<opponent>.red`).

```redcode
;redcode-94
;name Silk Bomber
;author OpenCode
;strategy 4-way silk paper replicator with three dat bombs per copy cycle
;assert CORESIZE==8000
        spl 1
        spl 1
        spl 1
        spl 1
silk    spl @0, 4507
        mov }-1, >-1
        mov bomb, >7123
        mov bomb, }4621
        mov bomb, {6784
        mov {silk, <silk3
silk3   jmp @0, 1479
bomb    dat <2667, <5334
        end
```

**Results (wins / losses / ties out of 100):**

| Opponent | W / L / T | Needed |
|---|---|---|
| stone | 96 / 4 / 0 | 75 |
| vampire | 100 / 0 / 0 | 75 |
| paper | 88 / 1 / 11 | 75 |
| snake | 59 / 1 / 40 | 33 |
| g2-clear | 43 / 46 / 11 | 33 |

**How it works:** The warrior splits into 16 processes, then runs a "silk" loop that keeps copying itself to new places in memory. Each pass of the loop also drops three DAT bombs elsewhere in memory. Copying makes it hard for stone and vampire to kill, and the bombs are what finish off small targets like g2-clear and the snake's imps.

**How I picked the numbers:** A plain version of this design passed against stone, vampire and paper but failed against snake (16 wins) and g2-clear (19 wins). Adding the extra bombs fixed that. I then ran a random search over the step and bomb offsets and kept the best set.

**How reliable it is:** The `-f` flag fixes the starting positions, so the test command gives the same numbers every time. Because the offsets were tuned under that flag, I also ran 500 battles per opponent with random starting positions. The win rates held: stone 95%, vampire 100%, paper 91%, snake 58%, g2-clear 40%. G2-clear has the thinnest margin: about 7 points above the 33% target with random starts, and 10 points above it under the test command.

I didn't change anything in `warriors/`, and I deleted the temporary test and search scripts.
